questions.title: StringBuffer Polymorphic Append Operations
questions.question: Create a `StringBuffer` instance and append multiple primitive and reference types (`String`, `int`, `char`, and `double`), then print the final buffer state and length.
questions.explanation: Unlike immutable `String` objects, `java.lang.StringBuffer` represents a mutable, thread-safe sequence of characters[cite: 18, 21]. Under the hood, `StringBuffer` manages an internal resizable character/byte array and provides overloaded `.append()` methods for all Java primitives, character arrays, and `Object` instances[cite: 21]. Calling `.append(10)` or `.append(3.14)` converts the argument into characters and copies them directly into the existing buffer, adjusting the internal `count` field without reallocating the container object[cite: 21]. This prevents temporary object creation on the heap during sequential text assembly[cite: 2, 18, 21].
hints: Instantiate a buffer using `StringBuffer sb = new StringBuffer("Java");`[cite: 21].
Chain or sequentially call `.append(" ")`, `.append(2026)`, `.append(':')`, and `.append(9.5)`[cite: 21].
Inspect the contents using `.toString()` and query character count via `.length()`[cite: 8, 21].

Result: Java 21: 9.5
Length: 14

questions.title: Positional Insertion with StringBuffer
questions.question: Demonstrate positional character insertion by using `StringBuffer.insert()` to insert text at the beginning (index 0) and in the middle of an existing buffer.
questions.explanation: The `StringBuffer.insert(int offset, ...)` method inserts text at a designated index within an existing character buffer[cite: 21]. When `.insert(0, text)` is invoked, the buffer shifts existing elements to the right starting from index 0 using native memory copy operations (`System.arraycopy`)[cite: 9, 15, 21]. If the insertion causes the character count to exceed the current capacity, the buffer grows automatically[cite: 21]. Inserting at a middle index shifts subsequent characters rightward by the length of the inserted token[cite: 21]. This allows in-place text modification without generating intermediate `String` objects[cite: 18, 21].
hints: Use `sb.insert(0, "Prefix ")` to prepend characters at the start of the buffer[cite: 21].
Locate an internal index and insert text into the middle: `sb.insert(offset, "Insert ")`[cite: 21].
Handle `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` by verifying `offset <= sb.length()`[cite: 18, 21].

Length:  21

questions.title: In-Place Reversal via StringBuffer
questions.question: Reverse an existing `StringBuffer` in place using `.reverse()` and print the buffer state before and after the operation.
questions.explanation: Reversing character sequences in place is supported natively by `StringBuffer.reverse()`[cite: 21]. Unlike immutable `String` instances where reversing requires manual loops or helper buffers, `StringBuffer.reverse()` mutates the underlying character array directly[cite: 12, 14, 18, 21]. It uses a two-pointer approach, swapping characters from outer boundaries inward until the pointers meet in the middle[cite: 5, 9, 19]. The operation handles surrogate pairs correctly and returns the same buffer reference (`this`), allowing further method chaining[cite: 9, 21].
hints: Create a buffer: `StringBuffer sb = new StringBuffer("Java");`[cite: 21].
Invoke `sb.reverse();` to swap characters directly in the internal array[cite: 21].

questions.title: Range Deletion and Single Character Removal
questions.question: Demonstrate character deletion in a `StringBuffer` by removing a range of characters with `.delete(start, end)` and removing an individual character with `.deleteCharAt(index)`.
questions.explanation: The `StringBuffer` class provides two deletion methods: `.delete(int start, int end)` and `.deleteCharAt(int index)`[cite: 21]. The range deletion method removes characters within the half-open interval `[start, end)` (inclusive of `start`, exclusive of `end`)[cite: 20, 21]. When characters are deleted, remaining elements are shifted left via `System.arraycopy`, and the internal length tracker decreases accordingly[cite: 9, 15, 21]. Similarly, `deleteCharAt(index)` shifts characters left by one position past the target index[cite: 21]. Both operations modify the existing buffer in place without allocating new container objects[cite: 18, 21].

questions.title: StringBuffer Capacity and Length Inspection
questions.question: Inspect and display the default initial capacity and length of a newly allocated `StringBuffer`, append text exceeding that capacity, and observe the updated values.
questions.explanation: In Java buffer classes, `length()` and `capacity()` represent two distinct concepts[cite: 21]. `length()` returns the number of active characters currently stored in the buffer[cite: 21]. `capacity()` returns the total number of characters the underlying allocated array can hold before needing reallocation[cite: 21]. When initialized via `new StringBuffer()`, the default capacity is 16 characters[cite: 21]. Appending text beyond 16 characters triggers growth logic (`newCapacity = (oldCapacity * 2) + 2`)[cite: 21]. The buffer allocates a larger array, copies existing characters over, and updates its capacity automatically[cite: 15, 21].

questions.explanation: Introduced in Java 5, `java.lang.StringBuilder` provides an unsynchronized, higher-performance alternative to `StringBuffer` for single-threaded string manipulation[cite: 21]. Both classes share an identical API inherited from `AbstractStringBuilder`[cite: 21]. Because `StringBuilder` mutator methods return `this`, operations can be chained fluently: `.append()`, `.insert()`, `.delete()`, and `.reverse()` execute sequentially on the same heap instance without method synchronization overhead[cite: 6, 9, 21].

Pre-allocating capacity avoids reallocation overhead when the approximate final string length is known in advance[cite: 18, 21]. When an append causes the character count to exceed the current capacity, `AbstractStringBuilder` expands the buffer using the growth formula `(oldCapacity * 2) + 2`[cite: 21]. If the required length exceeds that doubled threshold, the capacity expands directly to the required length[cite: 21].

questions.explanation: `StringBuffer` and `StringBuilder` share an identical API through their common superclass `AbstractStringBuilder`, but differ in synchronization[cite: 21]. Every public mutator method in `StringBuffer` (`append`, `insert`, `delete`, `reverse`) is declared with the `synchronized` keyword[cite: 21]. This acquires an intrinsic monitor lock on `this` during every operation, ensuring atomic mutations when multiple threads share a single buffer[cite: 6, 21]. `StringBuilder` omits synchronization entirely, eliminating locking overhead in single-threaded contexts[cite: 21].

Existing characters are copied to the new array via `System.arraycopy`, and the old array is discarded[cite: 9, 15, 21]. If the appended string requires more space than doubled capacity, the capacity expands directly to match the required length[cite: 21]. questions.title: Equality Evaluation: StringBuffer vs String
questions.question: Compare two distinct `StringBuffer` instances containing identical text using both `equals()` and `toString().equals()`, explaining why `StringBuffer` does not override `equals()`.
questions.explanation: `StringBuffer` (and `StringBuilder`) does not override `equals()` from `java.lang.Object`[cite: 21]. Consequently, calling `sb1.equals(sb2)` performs identity comparison (`sb1 == sb2`), checking whether both references point to the exact same heap address rather than comparing characters[cite: 5, 18, 21]. This design exists because buffers are mutable: changing characters would alter an object's equality and hash code, which breaks hash-based collections like `HashSet` and `HashMap`[cite: 8, 21]. To compare character contents, both buffers must be converted to `String` via `.toString()` before calling `.equals()`[cite: 18, 21].

A cleaner approach checks index boundaries inside the loop: if `i > 0`, the delimiter is prepended before the token, or appended conditionally for `i < array.length - 1`[cite: 3, 14]. This builds the formatted string directly in the buffer without requiring cleanup passes[cite: 21].

Multiple threads read the same `count`, write to the same array index, and overwrite each other's characters, resulting in a final length smaller than the expected total (or throwing `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`)[cite: 6, 18, 21]. In contrast, `StringBuffer` synchronizes every mutator method on `this`, serializing concurrent access and guaranteeing that all characters are written safely without lost updates[cite: 6, 21].

questions.title: Arbitrary-Precision Addition with StringBuilder
questions.question: Implement arbitrary-precision addition of two large numbers represented as strings using `StringBuilder` without using `BigInteger`.
questions.explanation: Standard 64-bit `long` integers cannot represent numbers with more than 19 digits without overflowing[cite: 5]. Adding arbitrarily large numbers requires simulating grade-school column addition using character buffers[cite: 21]. Two pointers start at the least significant digits (the right ends) of both strings and move leftward[cite: 9, 14]. On each step, the digits are converted to integers, added together with any carry from the previous column, and the resulting digit (`sum % 10`) is appended to a `StringBuilder`[cite: 14, 21]. The carry updates to `sum / 10`[cite: 7]. After the loop processes all digits and any final carry, reversing the buffer produces the final sum[cite: 21].

questions.question: Write an in-place markdown parser that strips bold (`**text**`), italics (`_text_`), and link markup (`[label](url) -> label`) using a `StringBuilder` cursor.
questions.explanation: Stripping markdown formatting (such as `**bold**`, `_italics_`, or `[title](url)`) for plain-text indexing can be implemented efficiently using a single-pass `StringBuilder` scanner[cite: 21]. A pointer iterates through the markdown text: when bold asterisks (`**`) or italic underscores (`_`) are encountered, the marker characters are skipped and the enclosed text is appended to the buffer[cite: 21]. For markdown links `[label](url)`, the parser extracts the link text inside brackets `[...]`, skips the target URL `(...)`, and appends only the label text to the buffer[cite: 20, 21]. This strips formatting in a single pass without regex compilation overhead[cite: 20].

questions.title: Zero-Garbage String Tokenizer
questions.question: Implement a high-throughput, zero-allocation tokenizer that parses delimited text streams using a reusable `StringBuilder` buffer to prevent heap garbage creation.
questions.explanation: Standard tokenizers (such as `String.split()` or `StringTokenizer`) allocate a new `String` object on the heap for every token extracted[cite: 18, 20]. In low-latency architectures (such as financial trading gateways or telemetry consumers), allocating millions of small token strings causes garbage collection pauses[cite: 2, 18]. A zero-allocation tokenizer avoids this by writing tokens into a single reusable `StringBuilder` buffer[cite: 21]. The scanner advances through the source text, copying characters between delimiters into the buffer and passing the buffer directly to a consumer before resetting its length with `sb.setLength(0)`[cite: 21]. This processes streams of tokens with zero intermediate heap allocations[cite: 2, 21].
